title: What If You Clipped Your Nails in Space?

scenes.text: What if you clipped your nails on the space station? Every clipping becomes a hazard.
With no gravity, clippings don't fall. They float around until they hit something, maybe someone's eye.
So in 2013, astronaut Chris Hadfield clipped his nails right over an air intake vent, letting the suction catch them.
Even then, one clipping escaped. He said he'd vacuum it up later.
Spacewalks are worse. Pressurized gloves press on the fingertips for hours, and nails can lift right off.
Astronauts with wider hands were about four times as likely to have a fingernail come loose. In space, even your nails need a plan.

description:
What if you clipped your nails in space? On the International Space Station, clippings float instead of falling, so in 2013 Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield trimmed his nails over an air intake vent whose suction pulls them into a filter.
Spacewalks are harder on nails: a 2010 MIT study (Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine) found astronauts with hand circumference above about 22.8 cm had roughly a 20% chance of fingernail delamination per spacewalk, against about 5% for smaller hands.
